title: The Book of Alison Knowles
text:
Stated Claim / Post Context:
The Book of Alison Knowles

A retrospective traces the language of bookmaking in her expansive work and its radical influence on American art.

Actual Article Body:
A retrospective traces the language of bookmaking in her expansive work and its radical influence on American art.

A retrospective of the late Fluxus artist Alison Knowles — known for performances, prints, sculptures, scores, and more — positions her as, of all things, an author. Curated by Karen Moss and traveling from the Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive (BAMPFA), the exhibition traces Knowles’s lifetime of output through the language of bookmaking — binding, paper, sequencing, narrative — and its radical influence on American art from the 1960s to today.

Knowles's capacity to absorb, translate, and communicate her surroundings proved pivotal in introducing the interdisciplinary, avant-garde, and performance-based tenets of Fluxus (meaning “to flow”) to American art in the early 1960s. Indeed, the exhibition’s first section introduces Knowles not only as a distinct artist, but also as an influential part of the larger movement invested in collaboration and ephemerality. New materialism, the relational aesthetics of the 1990s, and today's dialogic practices owe much to Fluxus, and the exhibition makes clear Knowles’s formative role in shaping contemporary artistic collaboration through iterative performances and works that use wide-ranging materials such as beans, shoes, and books.

Left: Installation view of by Alison Knowles: A Retrospective (1960–2022); right: Bruce Fleming, Knowles and others performing "Proposition #2: Make a Salad" at Festival of Misfits, Institute of Contemporary Arts, London, in 1962, photoreproduction on panel

At the entrance of this retrospective is a cluster of Knowles’s early works, including a reproduction of the newsprint-hued screenprint “Room” (1960), created with artist and composer George Brecht. The work is displayed above a vitrine with announcements from Knowles’s first shows, including her 1962 exhibition at Judson Gallery, the epicenter of the New York performance scene at the time. That year proved momentous for Knowles. She toured Europe with Fluxus founder George Maciunas, her collaborator (and on-again, off-again husband) Dick Higgins, and others. Footage from the collective’s time at Fluxus Festival in Wiesbaden, West Germany, is featured on a monitor nearby, as is a photograph from Knowles’s first performance of perhaps her best-known work, “Proposition #2: Make a Salad” (1962), at London’s Institute of Contemporary Art.

"Make a Salad" is the first of several works dealing with food represented here — including 1964’s “Variation #1: Make a Soup,” 1963–64’s scroll book “Bean Rolls,” and the recurring work “Identical Lunch,” first begun in the late 1960s — and encapsulates how banality was elevated to the extraordinary in Knowles’s hands. For the work, she gathers and then prepares a medley of greens, vegetables, and dressing for a group; as in her other collaborative, culinary-driven pieces, the point is as much how her audience and partners consume the work as it is her individual making of it.

Fluxus's use of cooperation, banality, and repeated gestures demonstrates the group’s abiding interest in shifting the avant-garde’s focus from solitary artistic genius to the aesthetics of group action. If Knowles’s preferred material seemed to be fiber (beans, greens, and paper), her interest was certainly in participation, as seen in the multi-media, jungle-gym-like sculptures “The Big Book” (1966) and “The Boat Book” (2014–15), or architecture, as in “The House of Dust” (1971). The latter, first presented at a New York housing development in 1969, is represented through photoreproductions of community activations in and out of the mound-like structure. On a more grandiose level, Knowles also created an infinite, computer-generated poem of randomized language to print on tractor-feed paper, as in “Live computer printout of the House of Dust (1971/2022), or to be disseminated from a helicopter, as with “Computer Poem Drop Event” (1971).
